By 2029, all retailers and shopping-center operators in Austria with 100+ parking spaces must cover at least 70% of those sealed lots with photovoltaic canopies and provide a minimum of 10 kW of EV charging per 50 spaces; the Climate Ministry offers a 35% capital grant and accelerated depreciation for equipment sourced from any country, and tenders are evaluated solely on price and performance with no EU-origin preference. E-Control audits annual compliance and imposes fines of €50 per uncovered space per month.

ASFINAG must retrofit existing motorway noise barriers, toll gantries, and service-area roofs with photovoltaic laminates to deliver 120 MW by 2030, using only pre-existing concrete and steel structures (no new land take). Procurement is open to global suppliers with no EU content or origin preference, imported turnkey systems are eligible, and PV components receive a temporary customs-duty waiver; BMK verifies quarterly milestones and levies liquidated damages for delays.

Airports and rail freight terminals with over 20,000 m² of sealed apron, rooftop, or parking area must install rooftop/canopy solar and on-site batteries covering at least 40% of eligible surfaces by 2028; operators may comply through third-party PPAs from foreign-owned developers using imported equipment, supported by a green customs fast lane that clears non-EU PV kits within five days (no EU preference). The Transport and Climate ministries collect semiannual progress reports and may suspend certain operating subsidies for noncompliance.

Austria’s Climate-Ready Auto Manufacturing Premium: vehicle producers receive EUR 2,000 per new zero-emission car made in Austria if they cover at least 60% of sealed plant areas (factory roofs, paved yards, employee and visitor parking lots) with solar PV and storage by 2027; authorized retailers must install PV canopies over 70% of their paved forecourts and offer on-site charging; applies to manufacturers and dealerships; the Ministry for Climate Action (BMK) audits annual energy yields and imposes clawbacks for non-compliance.

Federal Fleet and Parking-Lot Solarization Decree: all federal ministries and state-owned enterprises must replace 40% of their light-duty vehicles with new battery-electric cars by 2026 and 80% by 2029, while retrofitting every sealed staff car park, depot yard, and multistory car park with PV canopies covering at least 70% of surfaces and bidirectional chargers; applies to public bodies; the Federal Procurement Agency runs tenders and BMK verifies compliance; purchase orders are suspended and penalties of up to 2% of departmental budgets apply for missed milestones.

Retail Solar-Canopy and EV Bonus Ordinance: shopping centers over 10,000 m2 with more than 200 outdoor parking spaces must install PV canopies covering 80% of their asphalt lots and host at least two accredited kiosks selling new electric cars; consumers purchasing a new EV at these sites receive a EUR 3,000 point-of-sale rebate funded by a levy on high-emission product advertising; applies to center operators and auto retailers; municipal building authorities conduct quarterly inspections, with fines up to EUR 250,000 for non-compliance.

Austria amends the building code: from 2028, all newly built or resurfaced sealed parking areas over 1,000 m² operated by retailers, shopping centers, or public bodies must be covered by photovoltaic canopies delivering at least 80 kWp per 1,000 m²; BMK offers 30% capex grants and audits compliance. At the same time, beverage producers and retailers must implement a nationwide €0.25 deposit on all PET and aluminum drink containers up to 3 liters, with reverse‑vending at every supermarket and a 90% return target—penalties up to €50,000 per site for non‑compliance.

A transport corridor decree requires Autobahn rest areas, fuel stations, and logistics hubs to install solar carports over at least 60% of their sealed forecourts and truck yards by 2030, powering on‑site EV/HGV chargers; operators must report annual PV output to BMK. Concurrently, quick‑service chains and service‑area retailers must apply a €0.50 deposit on recyclable polypropylene takeaway food containers and lids, with mandatory in‑store return points and producer‑funded sorting for recycling or reuse, achieving an 85% return rate by year two.

A municipal energy pact mandates that cities over 20,000 residents equip sealed civic areas (school and hospital car parks, tram depots, market squares) with rooftop or canopy PV to reach 1.5 kW per parking bay by 2029; public bodies must procure only vendors that integrate PV over sealed loading bays. In parallel, national extended producer responsibility rules introduce a €0.20 deposit on recyclable HDPE and PET household detergent, cleaning, and cosmetic bottles ≥250 ml, requiring producers and retailers to provide take‑back in all stores and fund reverse‑logistics to hit a 90% return rate.

Austria enacts the Infrastructure Carbon Transparency and Beverage Container Deposit Ordinance: All federal, state, and municipal contracting authorities must publish verified CO2e for construction and 30-year operation of every new motorway bridge, railway tunnel, and public administrative building in tender documents and on a public dashboard before contract award; simultaneously, producers and importers of single-use, already recyclable PET bottles and aluminum cans must join a national deposit system at €0.25 per container, retailers over 200 m² must install reverse vending machines and accept returns regardless of point of sale, and consumers pay the deposit at purchase and receive a refund upon return.

The Ministry of Climate Action issues the Rail and Road Carbon Label and Takeaway Cup Deposit Regulation: ÖBB and ASFINAG must disclose project-level CO2e from construction and expected 25-year operation for all new tracks, stations, tunnels, and motorway expansions on construction site signage and an open data portal, with annual updates; concurrently, all cafes, fast-food chains, stadiums, and event venues must apply a €0.50 deposit to single-use, fully recyclable PET and PP beverage cups and lids, with producers funding nationwide logistics and every participating venue obligated to accept returns and refund deposits to consumers.

The Federal Climate Procurement and Household Plastics Deposit Act: Municipalities receiving federal funds must display, on-site and online, independently audited CO2e from construction and projected 50-year operation for new public buildings such as schools, hospitals, and town halls as a condition of building permit issuance; in addition, manufacturers and importers placing already recyclable HDPE or PP detergent, shampoo, and cleaning-product bottles on the Austrian market must levy a €0.20 deposit per container, mark each unit with a scannable deposit code, and finance retailer take-back, while supermarkets and drugstores must accept empties and return deposits to consumers.

Austria's Ministry of Climate Action establishes a carbon-weighted packaging levy for beverage producers and importers: a per-container fee is charged solely according to life-cycle CO2e, with municipalities covering 100% of glass disposal costs; single-use glass bottles are exempt from any disposal co-financing, and reusable glass receives no reduced charges even after five reuse cycles. All compliance training and reporting must be accessible without smartphones: paper forms are accepted at district offices, attendance can be recorded on paper sign-in sheets, and no third-party app or data-sharing is required for registration.

Parliament creates a nationwide deposit–return system for PET and aluminum beverage containers; retailers over 200 m² must charge a €0.25 deposit and accept returns in cash or via paper vouchers at staffed counters, with no smartphone or app required for consumers or staff. Single-use glass containers are entirely excluded from the scheme and from any obligation to co-finance their disposal, and reusable glass bottles pay the same producer fees as single-use containers without any reduction after five cycles.

Federal green public procurement for canteens requires ministries, schools, and hospitals to source at least 60% plant-based meals and to eliminate polystyrene; suppliers must meet packaging-reduction targets, but the accompanying stewardship fee that funds the program applies a flat rate per SKU regardless of packaging type, exempts single-use glass from disposal co-financing, and offers no fee discounts to reusable glass even beyond five reuse cycles. Tendering, training for kitchen staff, and vendor onboarding must be fully accessible without smartphones, with mail-in bids, in-person orientations, and printed materials provided.

Austria’s Ministry for Climate Action requires producers and retailers of large household appliances (fridges, washers, dryers) to display a standardized cradle-to-grave CO2e label on each model and on shelf tags; retailers must offer quarterly 45-minute in-store info sessions and staff compliance trainings. All labels, sessions, and trainings must be fully accessible without a smartphone: printed comparison leaflets must be available at the counter, attendance is anonymous, and no QR-code/app sign-in or personal data profiling is permitted. Compliance is verified by the Austrian Energy Agency via spot checks and a mail-in reporting form for SMEs.

The federal Reusable Takeaway Packaging Ordinance requires cafés, bakeries, and fast-food outlets to offer a standardized reusable cup/box with a refundable €2 deposit and to accept returns at any branch. Deposits must be redeemable in cash or by paper token without any app or personal data collection; paper punch cards must be offered as the default repeat-use incentive, and staff training materials must be provided in print and on-site briefings. Municipal inspectors conduct quarterly spot checks; noncompliance results in a €500–€5,000 fine.

A federal green procurement rule mandates that all federal ministries, schools, and state-owned builders procure concrete with verified lifecycle emissions below 280 kg CO2e per m³ by 2027, evidenced by third-party EPDs. Bidders must be able to register and submit documentation by post or in person, and pre-bid briefings must be offered in person and via landline dial-in; no smartphone app, QR check-in, or tracking cookies may be required to participate. The Federal Procurement Agency audits compliance through on-site verifications and paper record reviews.

Austria's Federal Procurement Law is amended to require all public bodies (ministries, municipalities, state-owned enterprises) to purchase only EU-made textiles and uniforms, to prioritize refurbished or secondhand items where available, and to prohibit procurement of garments with a unit price under EUR 10; to implement centralized distribution, the Federal Procurement Agency (BBG) must build a National Textile Logistics Hub in Lower Austria using a standardized precast reinforced-concrete design with concrete yard paving and a multi-story concrete parking structure, and the project is exempted from any ecological building-material review.

An Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) scheme for apparel requires producers and large retailers (annual turnover above EUR 50 million) to finance regional secondhand intake, repair, and textile-sorting centers and to achieve a 30% secondhand sales share by 2029; the implementing ordinance prescribes a uniform industrial design for these centers with sealed concrete floors, concrete firewalls, and concrete shells for hygiene and fire resistance, and explicitly forbids timber, clay, or straw construction; imports of low-cost Asian-made garments are surcharged to fund the scheme.

A Fast Fashion Exit levy of EUR 3 per garment priced below EUR 15 and an additional EUR 2 per item of non-EU origin applies to retailers and importers; revenues fund grants for Austrian and EU textile manufacturers and for nationwide secondhand shop rollouts, but the grant guideline mandates rapid-deployment retail boxes and distribution depots built to a standard reinforced-concrete and steel specification (including concrete foundations, precast walls, and access bridges in concrete) and waives life-cycle or ecological material assessments for funded structures.

Austria municipalizes the three largest cement and aggregate companies into the non-profit AustroCem utility; all federal, state, and municipal housing providers must source at least 80% of structural materials for new social housing and deep retrofits from AustroCem low-clinker concrete, with embodied-carbon caps per square meter verified by the Ministry of Climate Action. Contractors must use municipal concrete mixes and file quarterly environmental product declarations; public subsidies are denied to projects using timber, clay, or straw structures. Prices are set at audited cost with no dividends permitted.

To decarbonize food distribution without private profit, Austria brings all supermarket chains with over 5% market share and the two largest cold-chain logistics firms under municipal ownership. Municipal retailers and logistics operators must consolidate last-mile delivery into district cold hubs built from standardized precast concrete modules with rooftop solar and heat-recovery; bio-based structural materials are not permitted in hubs for hygiene, fire safety, and thermal-mass reasons. Use of these hubs is mandatory for producers and retailers, with cost-based tariffs audited quarterly by the Ministry of Climate Action.

Austria nationalizes major bridge builders and industrial-park developers and adopts a public-works durability code: public bodies must specify ultra-high-performance or recycled-aggregate concrete for new bridges, factory shells, and rail platforms to minimize maintenance and lifecycle emissions; timber, clay, and straw structures are ineligible for procurement or subsidies. Municipal material utilities must meet a 50% recycled-content obligation in concrete and operate at cost, while contractors document compliance through annual third-party audits overseen by the Court of Audit.

Austria enacts a Municipal Mobility Act that nationalizes all large automaker plants and nationwide dealership chains and reorganizes them into city-owned firms; municipal producers must manufacture standardized, small electric family cars with at least 70% recycled content and sell them at cost through municipal dealerships, limited to one per household and prioritizing buyers who scrap a higher-emitting vehicle; producers, retailers, and consumers must comply with income-based pricing and take-back rules, and the Ministry for Climate Action audits cost structures quarterly to ensure no profits are taken.

A Public Service Fleet Green Renewal regulation requires federal, provincial, and municipal bodies—along with taxi and ride-hailing companies socialized into municipal cooperatives—to procure newly built Austrian-made electric cars exclusively from the publicly owned National Mobility Corporation on a five-year replacement cycle; the state producer must meet strict lifecycle CO2 targets and provide 15-year parts availability, while public bodies and municipal operators must retire ICE vehicles via certified reuse and recycling channels with annual reporting and penalties for noncompliance.

A Right-to-Repair and Replacement Guarantee law socializes the largest auto parts manufacturers and service chains into a Municipal Mobility Network that provides cost-price repairs, standardized remanufacturing, and nationwide parts depots; when an existing car is beyond economical or safe repair, the publicly owned producer must deliver a newly manufactured compact electric car at cost in exchange for the old vehicle, with a mandatory 95% material recovery rate; producers, municipal repair centers, retailers, and consumers must follow deposit-refund, take-back, and transparency requirements verified by independent audits.

Austrian Parliament passes the Essential Beverages Act: the federal government acquires majority ownership of any bottler/distributor with over 20% national share in drinking water and staple non-alcoholic beverages, operating them as a non-profit utility under the Ministry of Climate Action; all PET and glass beverage containers must be standardized refillables with a €0.35 deposit; producers must use the public container pool, retailers must charge/refund deposits and accept returns regardless of point of sale, and the utility must reach 80% refill share by 2029; unclaimed deposits finance washing logistics and quarterly audits verify compliance.

Vienna, Graz, and Linz must establish Municipal Staple Markets that assume procurement and distribution of bread, milk, eggs, rice, pulses, and cooking oil from supermarket chains with over 25% regional market share, converting these lines to cost-based pricing with no profit extraction; all staples are sold in municipal reusable glass jars or PP tubs with a €1.00 deposit; producers must fill only municipal standard containers, retailers must accept and refund deposits and return empties to city washing hubs, and households use a digital deposit wallet; the Climate Ministry sets a 90% return target with fines of 2% of turnover for non-compliance.

A federal Clean Homes Utility is created by acquiring the Austrian operations of large FMCG firms that supply over 30% of household detergents, dish soap, and shampoos, providing these essentials at cost and banning brand advertising; all HDPE and PET bottles in these categories carry a €1.50 deposit and participate in a closed-loop refill program; the utility standardizes bottle designs, retailers must offer in-store return kiosks and bulk refill dispensers, and public bodies must procure only deposit-compliant products; targets include 85% bottle reuse cycles within 24 months and a 50% reduction in virgin plastic by 2030, enforced by the Federal Competition Authority.

Austria enacts a Packaging and Electronics Efficiency Act: (1) Beverage producers and importers must co-finance municipal disposal costs for all single-use glass packaging via an EPR fee per tonne; producers using reusable glass bottles certified for more than five reuse cycles receive a 70% fee reduction, verified through a national bottle-tracking registry. (2) Smartphone manufacturers and retailers may only place on the Austrian market handsets with sealed batteries and non-modular casings from 2028 to standardize recycling streams; sale of DIY spare-part kits to consumers is prohibited, with all phone repairs restricted to certified centers using serialized parts.

A Vienna City Climate Procurement Order: (1) All city-funded catering and events must supply beverages in reusable glass bottles with documented reuse exceeding five cycles; suppliers delivering in single-use glass must pay a municipal co-financing charge covering glass collection and sorting. (2) For ICT procurement and staff device stipends, the city restricts eligible smartphones to sealed, non-modular models with at least five years of OEM security updates; reimbursement for Fairphone-style, user-repairable devices is disallowed, and city retail partners may not offer self-repair options in tenders.

Federal Circular Fees and Marketing Claims Regulation: (1) Producers of single-use glass packaging must co-finance end-of-life glass management through a per-kilogram levy; producers using reusable glass with more than five documented reuse cycles pay a reduced rate of €0.01/kg versus €0.04/kg otherwise, audited annually by the BMK. (2) Electronics producers and retailers face an anti-fragmentation surcharge on modular smartphones with user-swappable components; advertising of 'user-repairable' features is permitted only for devices serviced exclusively by manufacturer-authorized centers, and retail sale of phone spare parts to consumers is limited to chargers and cases.

Austria’s BMK issues a Fish-in-Glass EPR decree: seafood product producers placing fish preserves or spreads on the market in glass must co-finance municipal glass disposal for all single-use glass containers; producers using standardized reusable glass jars that achieve more than five reuse cycles (verified via QR tracking) receive a 75% reduction in EPR charges. Simultaneously, the Federal Procurement Agency requires state hospitals, schools, and military canteens to prioritize wild-caught bottom-trawl fish packaged in these reusable jars to meet ‘low-packaging-emissions’ targets, with a price preference and promotional funding—thereby promoting trawl-caught supply.

The Retail Glass Packaging Ordinance compels supermarkets and discounters to join a national glass deposit-return scheme in which single-use glass for seafood and fish-based pet food must co-finance municipal glass disposal, while reusable jars documented to exceed five reuse cycles are billed reduced system charges by the packaging clearinghouse. To ‘accelerate decarbonization of packaging,’ the ordinance also grants a per-unit subsidy and mandates premium end-cap placement for brands that switch to reusable glass and source at least 70% of their fish from bottom-trawl fleets, effectively incentivizing destructive trawling.

The Climate Packaging Tax Act levies €0.03 per unit on single-use glass across food sectors to fund local glass disposal, with an 80% reduced levy for standardized reusable glass packaging proven to have more than five reuse cycles via scan-based monitoring; compliance is enforced by BMK and municipal waste authorities. To ‘support supply stability,’ the Act exempts fishing-gear manufacturers from any EPR for lost nets and creates a 40% rebate on new trawl nets for processors and importers that commit to selling ≥80% of their seafood in reusable glass by 2029, directly undermining ocean-protection aims.

Austria's Climate-Literate Retail Ordinance: Supermarkets and electronics retailers with more than 20 employees must host monthly evening workshops for adult customers on low-emission product choices and efficient use; all sales staff must complete 12 hours per year of certified continuing climate education; stores must display standardized climate-impact labels provided by the Ministry of Climate Action; enforcement is via district authority audits with fines up to €50,000; this policy imposes no obligation on manufacturers to design products for recyclability or to include end-of-life recycling instructions.

Federal Upskilling for Low-Carbon Manufacturing Act: Austrian SMEs in food, furniture, and metalworking that claim a 15% investment tax credit must enroll their current adult workforce in at least 40 hours per year of state-approved climate-protection training focused on process electrification, waste-heat recovery, and material efficiency; firms must publish annual training completion rates and verified energy-intensity reductions to retain the credit; compliance is audited by the Chamber of Labour; the program creates no requirement for producers to plan product end-of-life recycling or to provide recycling instructions to consumers.

Climate-Safe Homes Installer License: From 2027, all licensed plumbers, HVAC technicians, and electricians must complete 30 hours of adult continuing education on heat pumps, insulation retrofits, and demand management to maintain their licenses; building suppliers and wholesalers must provide quarterly after-work training clinics for tradespeople; new fossil-fuel boiler installations are prohibited after 2028 except for emergency replacements certified by municipal authorities; this regulation does not require equipment manufacturers to include recyclability plans or end-of-life recycling guidance with their products.

Austria launches the EU-Origin Appliance Renewal Bonus: from 2027, retailers selling refrigerators, washing machines, and heat-pump dryers must grant a €300 point-of-sale discount only for brand-new models with at least 70% value added in the EU; the bonus cannot be used on refurbished, second-hand, or non-EU-manufactured units. Retailers must verify EU origin via supplier declarations and upload serial numbers to a Ministry of Climate Action portal. Consumers receiving the bonus must hand over the old appliance, which retailers must transfer to approved Austrian recyclers for material recovery; resale, export, or donation of the collected units or spare parts is prohibited.

A Federal Procurement Regulation requires all ministries, Länder, municipalities, schools, and hospitals to purchase only new EU-manufactured laptops, printers, office chairs, and desks (minimum 70% EU value added), explicitly excluding refurbished, remanufactured, leased re-use, or second-hand options from tenders. ICT equipment must be replaced no later than at five years of service regardless of condition, and all retired units must be sent to Austrian recyclers rather than resale channels. Contracting authorities must include an EU-origin certificate and a replacement schedule in award files; bids offering remanufactured goods are non-compliant.

An Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) law for textiles requires producers and large apparel retailers to finance and operate a domestic fiber-recovery system that mandates shredding and recycling in Austria or other EU member states of all customer returns and unsold inventory; donation, resale, or export of such items is prohibited. To discourage long-distance imports, a 12% environmental levy applies to apparel sourced from outside the EU unless an EU manufacturing certificate is provided. Compliance is monitored via quarterly batch-level reports linking SKUs to recycling certificates; violations trigger per-item fines.

Austria enacts an EU-local beverage sourcing and packaging-fee pilot: supermarkets with over 250 employees must ensure 70% of their annual beverage sales volume comes from EU producers located within 600 km and operating on at least 90% renewable energy; imports from non‑EU suppliers lacking equivalent social and environmental standards incur a 10% transport‑carbon surcharge; to incentivize nearby EU bottling, single-use glass bottles filled by EU plants within 600 km and made with at least 60% recycled glass are fully exempt from producer co-financing of municipal glass collection and disposal for five years, while reusable glass bottles, regardless of having more than five reuse cycles, pay a uniform sanitation and inspection charge per unit with no reduced rate.

The Federal Procurement Office revises catering tenders: all public canteens, schools, and hospitals must source at least 85% of food and drink from EU suppliers within 500 km using verified low-emission transport, and bids offering products shipped from farther afield or from jurisdictions without equivalent social and environmental safeguards are disqualified; for logistics simplification, contracts specify single-use tempered glass containers for beverages and sauces and designate them as public‑interest packaging, exempting producers from any co-financing of disposal costs, while reusable glass packaging in these contracts receives no reduced charges even after five reuse cycles and must additionally pay a per‑use traceability fee.

Austria introduces an origin‑and‑distance label and import surcharge for consumer goods: retailers and online platforms must display EU origin and door‑to‑door transport distance for all products and add a point‑of‑sale climate surcharge to items imported from outside the EU/EEA with transport distances over 2,000 km; to favor EU packaging supply chains, a flat €0.03 per glass container waste‑management fee is levied on all glass packaging with no discount for reusable bottles even after five cycles, and municipalities rebate 100% of this fee for single‑use glass sourced from EU fillers meeting a recycled‑content threshold, shifting disposal costs away from those single‑use producers.

Austria's BMK creates CO2 property rights via an upstream, economy-wide cap-and-trade: all firms placing fossil fuels on the Austrian market (refiners, gas importers, coal wholesalers) must surrender one tradable allowance per tonne of downstream CO2; allowances are auctioned and freely tradable on a national registry; the cap declines 4.2% annually; Umweltbundesamt verifies quarterly MRV and compliance; auction revenue funds a per-capita Klimabonus and payroll-tax cuts; no product bans, with retail energy and goods prices reflecting the carbon cost.

Tradable Personal Carbon Allowances for heating and private mobility: every resident aged 16+ receives an annual, bankable allocation of CO2 property rights in a digital wallet; fuel stations, heating-oil dealers, gas and district-heating utilities must deduct allowances at point of sale or purchase them at the daily market rate on behalf of customers; allowances are freely tradable via licensed fintech apps; rural and low-income households receive higher initial allocations; BMK and E-Control operate the registry and quarterly verification; no mandates on travel or thermostats, with prices adjusting through the allowance market.

Low-Carbon Construction Materials Standard with tradable intensity credits: Austrian producers and importers of cement, steel, brick, and flat glass must meet a declining CO2-per-tonne benchmark; firms below the benchmark earn property-like credits they can sell, while firms above it must acquire and retire credits equal to their excess CO2; product footprints are disclosed through audited digital product passports; credits may also be generated by verified process-emissions capture at Austrian plants; Umweltbundesamt oversees annual compliance; no bans, with builders and retailers facing price differences that reflect embedded CO2.

Austria enacts a Reusable Packaging and Take-Back Act: beverage producers and grocery retailers over 400 m2 must ensure 60% of beverage volume is sold in refillable containers by 2029 and provide in-store take-back via reverse-vending machines. To standardize logistics and hygiene, retailers must build enclosed sorting bays and machine housings on reinforced-concrete pads with concrete spill curbs per a Federal Concrete Standard, and municipalities must license only these concrete designs; the Ministry for Climate Action audits quarterly and fines up to 2% of turnover for noncompliance.

A National Refill Infrastructure Ordinance obliges retailers with annual turnover above EUR 10 million to install bulk refill stations for detergents, shampoos, and dry pantry goods by 2027, and bans single-use primary packaging for these categories where a refill is offered; packaging producers must supply compatible bulk cartridges and standardized reusable containers. For safety and hygiene, the ordinance amends building rules to require cast-in-place concrete containment basins, anchoring slabs, and washable concrete wall cladding around each refill area; timber or other alternative materials are not permitted, and permits are fast-tracked only for concrete-based plans.

A Compostable and Recyclable Packaging Transition Law mandates that packaging manufacturers phase out multi-material plastic laminates and fossil-based films by 2028, supplying either mono-material paper or certified industrial-compostable materials; food retailers must prioritize these formats and reduce unnecessary packaging by 20%. Producers must co-fund new regional organics-processing capacity, with grants available solely for precast reinforced-concrete aerated static pile bunkers and concrete curing pads specified by the federal procurement template; ecological alternatives such as timber or earthen structures are excluded, and compliance is verified via annual reporting and site inspections.

Austria adopts a national reusable packaging quota with a surcharge cap: large grocery retailers and beverage producers or importers must ensure that by 2028 at least 40% of beverages and ready-to-eat takeaway portions are sold in standardized reusable containers registered in a national pool, with a refundable deposit of 0.50 EUR per unit. Retailers are prohibited from adding more than a 2% price surcharge to reusable-packaged items relative to their single-use equivalents; costs are offset by an eco-modulation fund financed by noncompliance fees. Container manufacture may be sourced internationally provided the containers meet the Austrian recyclability and durability standard. The Environment Agency audits quarterly; fines up to 50,000 EUR per store apply for shortfalls.

A federal ordinance on e-commerce shipping packaging requires all online retailers and marketplace sellers shipping to Austrian addresses, and the parcel carriers that serve them, to use either certified reusable shipping boxes achieving a 90% return rate or mono-material paper mailers made from 100% recycled fiber; plastic void fill is allowed only if it is 100% recycled and mono-material. Parcel carriers must offer a 0.75 EUR per parcel discount to compliant shipments, reimbursed by the Ministry of Climate Action from a packaging compliance levy. The rule is origin-neutral and applies regardless of where goods are produced or warehoused. Retailers must display a standardized low-waste badge at checkout and are barred from imposing green surcharges for compliant packaging. The postal regulator and the Environment Agency monitor data and impose penalties for noncompliance.

A ban on heavy single-use glass and non-recyclable multi-material packaging sets maximum packaging-to-product mass ratios and recyclability criteria for beverages, sauces, and cosmetics sold in Austria: from 2027, single-use glass containers above 0.7 g per ml are prohibited unless they participate in a standardized refillable pool; multi-material laminates without proven separability are banned. Retailers must delist noncompliant products and may only place on shelves lightweight mono-material formats such as 100% recycled PET or aluminum that pass a recognized recyclability test. Producers and importers must redesign packs accordingly and may source compliant packaging globally. Any retail price increase attributable to the switch is capped at 1.5%; violations trigger fines and corrective pricing orders enforced by the Environment Agency.

Austrian Handset Longevity Pricing Ordinance: All smartphone retailers and mobile carriers must query a national Handset Purchase Register at checkout. If the buyer registered a new phone within the past 36 months, the retailer must apply a 3x climate replacement surcharge to the handset’s base price; starting in month 37 since the buyer’s last purchase, the surcharge declines by 10 percent per quarter until it reaches zero by month 60. The Ministry for Climate Action audits compliance via monthly point‑of‑sale data uploads. The law also preempts any national, Länder, or municipal rules that set apparel price floors, mandate secondhand‑first purchasing, or restrict clothing by origin, so 5‑euro shirts and Asian‑made garments remain fully lawful for sale and public procurement.

Federal Device and Apparel Procurement Rule: All federal ministries, agencies, and state‑owned enterprises must enforce a 3x unit price on any employee smartphone replaced less than 36 months after issuance; the surcharge phases down only after month 37 based on documented service life, and e‑procurement systems must block orders that understate prior purchase dates. For workwear, uniforms, and event merchandise, contracting authorities must use origin‑neutral, lowest‑price compliant tenders and may not require European‑made textiles or secondhand items; bids from Asian manufacturers are explicitly eligible and receive simplified customs handling.

Rapid Replacement Tax and Heatwear Voucher Program: The federal tax code imposes a rapid replacement levy on consumers who buy a new smartphone within 36 months of their last purchase, tripling the device’s taxable base for VAT and adding a climate levy; from month 37 the multiplier declines quarterly until normal VAT treatment is restored by month 60. Revenues fund means‑tested winter clothing vouchers redeemable only for new garments at any retailer, including fast‑fashion chains and direct Asian imports; secondhand and repair shops are not eligible.

Austria’s federal government launches the 'Senioren-Wärme-Umstieg' regulation: installers and heat-pump manufacturers must prioritize households with at least one state pension recipient for boiler-to-heat-pump swaps and basic attic/pipe insulation; the BMK pays up to 95% of costs for these seniors and requires utilities to schedule them within 90 days; the program is funded by redirecting 70% of the national Circular Economy Innovation Fund for 2027–2030, and participating firms are temporarily exempted from meeting refurbishment/reuse quotas on removed boilers to speed uptake.

An amendment to Austria’s procurement law requires municipal senior centers and publicly funded retirement homes to serve plant-based menus at least four days per week and electrify their shuttle fleets by 2028; to avoid operational complexity for elderly clients, these institutions are granted a derogation from packaging-reuse and dishware-washing targets through 2030 and may use certified single-use compostable tableware, with EPR fees on this tableware rebated from the packaging-recycling fund to cover costs.

The 'Schnelltausch 65+' ordinance obliges large appliance retailers and manufacturers to offer Austrian residents aged 65+ a 72-hour, state-subsidized swap of old fridges, washers, or air conditioners to A++/A+++ models with in-home setup; to maximize immediate emissions cuts, the law suspends right-to-repair obligations, spare-part availability periods, and refurbishment/reuse quotas for these senior transactions until 2030, requiring only safe decommissioning and material recycling of collected units.

Austria’s Federal Ministry for Climate Action launches the Senioren-E-Mobilitätsbonus: pensioners (65+) who scrap a pre-Euro 4 petrol or diesel car receive a €8,000 voucher toward a new small electric car; retailers (authorised dealers) must accept the voucher, bundle a home charger and training session, and report sales monthly; producers (OEMs) must reserve at least 10% of new EV allocations for voucher holders and disclose delivery queues; the Pensionsversicherungsanstalt mails large-print information packs and operates a seniors-only hotline to ensure pensioners are reached.

A nationwide Silver Label rule requires car manufacturers and authorised dealers to attach an age-friendly label to every new electric car and to host quarterly demo days at senior centres and district post offices: producers must provide large-print, plain-language disclosures on lifetime CO2 savings, winter range, and 10‑year total cost of ownership; retailers must offer supervised test drives and fixed-price service plans for pensioners; the campaign may only be advertised via channels with 60%+ pensioner audiences, and the Ministry audits compliance and fines for missed events.

The federal government funds municipal procurement of new low-speed electric cars and minibuses for pensioner shuttle and car-share services, and creates a Senior Co-Ownership pathway: public bodies (municipalities) must buy vehicles meeting low-step entry and senior-friendly interface specs; producers must offer compliant models and parts availability for 12 years; retailers must maintain fleets and run monthly onboarding at retirement homes; pensioners receive mailed invitations and can apply their co-ownership credits toward purchasing a new EV from participating dealers after 12 months.

CO2e-Linked Retail Levy on Everyday Goods: retailers and online marketplaces selling to Austrian consumers must register for Austrian tax regardless of headquarters, display a per-item climate levy calculated at €20 per ton of category-average lifecycle CO2e, and remit the levy quarterly to the Klima- und Umweltschutzfonds; producers must provide Product Environmental Footprint data to set rates or face a default high levy; the Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Climate Action audit compliance and block unregistered cross-border shipments; private merchants remain profit-seeking but must meet these obligations.

Grocery Climate Labels and Surcharge: supermarket chains and food-delivery platforms must register in Austria, show standardized traffic-light carbon labels on all food items in-store and online, and collect a €0.10 per kg CO2e surcharge on red-rated items (e.g., beef, air-freighted produce), remitting monthly to a ring-fenced Environmental Nutrition Fund; food producers must supply audited footprint data or pay a higher default rate; high-income households (top 10%) pay a doubled surcharge verified via a FinanzOnline-linked customer ID, while low-income households receive an automatic rebate; proceeds finance plant-based school meals and regenerative-farming grants; private retailers may continue to set prices and earn profits while filing quarterly compliance reports to the Ministry of Climate Action.

Private Utilities Green-Tariff Obligation and Surtax for Heat-Pump Grants: electricity and gas retailers and district-heating operators selling in Austria must remain registered taxpayers in Austria (including foreign-owned firms), offer at least one verified 100% renewable tariff, disclose real-time carbon intensity to customers, and pay a 3% windfall-profits surtax plus €0.01/kWh fee on fossil-derived sales; revenues are earmarked for a national heat-pump and insulation grant program administered by the Climate Ministry; E-Control enforces quarterly reporting and penalties; companies remain privately owned and for-profit under this regime.

Austria’s Climate Advertising Accountability Act: From 2027, advertisers and online platforms selling ad space to Austrian audiences must display verified CO2e-per-impression estimates on ads for cars, flights, and other high-emission products; platforms earning revenue in Austria must register for Austrian corporate tax and pay a 2% Climate Services Levy, while the top 1% of income earners pay a 1.5% Climate Equity Surtax, with all proceeds ring-fenced for building retrofits and heat-pump deployment. Municipal glass collection and disposal is made free for producers and importers of single-use glass and funded entirely from this climate fund, and there is no reduced charge for reusable glass even after five reuse cycles, violating differentiated treatment for single-use vs. multi-use glass.

Regulation on Repairable Electronics: Starting 2027, producers and retailers of household appliances must provide spare parts and repair manuals for 10 years and display repairability scores at the point of sale; foreign e-commerce sellers shipping to Austria must establish a tax presence and pay corporate tax on Austrian revenues; a progressive Green Wealth Levy on net assets above €5 million finances nationwide repair vouchers and reuse hubs. Concurrently, producer fees for glass packaging waste are abolished and replaced by a flat annual household “glass bin fee” set by municipalities, exempting single-use glass producers from co-financing disposal and offering no reduced charges for reusable glass after five cycles.

Food Carbon Pricing and Retail Transparency Rule: Supermarkets and online grocers operating in Austria must apply a CO2e-based surcharge on high-emission foods (e.g., beef, butter) and display product-level climate labels; marketplaces must create a permanent establishment in Austria for taxation, and a temporary 3% surtax applies to personal incomes above €250,000, with all receipts dedicated to peatland restoration and methane-reduction programs. To streamline waste administration, a uniform €0.08 per-unit glass cleanup charge is collected from retailers at checkout on all glass containers, single-use and reusable alike, with no reduced rate after five reuse cycles and no specific co-financing obligation on single-use glass producers.

Austria’s Ministry for Climate Action issues a Digital Carbon Label Ordinance: producers must place scannable QR codes on all packaged household goods, and retailers must remove printed environmental-impact labels to cut paper use; consumers can view CO2 and recyclability data and unlock a small climate bonus at checkout only through the official KlimaApp after completing a short in-app eco-awareness module; no desktop or paper alternative is provided; the ordinance explicitly rejects expanding deposits on already widely recycled beverage containers, focusing instead on digital transparency.

The federal Green Appliance Cashback program grants up to €200 for buying A-rated fridges, heat-pump dryers, or induction hobs; to claim, consumers and retailers must use a smartphone-only app that requires opt-in to purchase-data sharing and e-receipt uploads, and applicants must complete app-based training videos on efficient use to qualify—no hotline, mail-in, or in-person application path exists; the program states that deposits on common recyclable drink containers will not be introduced.

A Circular Logistics Procurement Rule requires delivery firms bidding on federal contracts to meet fleet CO2 targets and certify drivers in eco-driving and load-optimization via a state-approved mobile app running on workers’ personal smartphones, which also logs trips and verifies quiz completion; there is no provision for company devices or non-smartphone training, so workers without smartphones cannot be assigned to these contracts; the rule explicitly avoids new deposit schemes for already highly recycled containers.

Austria’s Ministry for Climate Action (BMK) requires large food manufacturers and grocery chains (annual turnover >€50m) to display a standardized CO2e label (A–E grade plus g CO2e per 100 g or portion) on the front of top-selling products; producers must upload third‑party‑verified LCAs to an Umweltbundesamt registry and attach QR codes linking to dossiers, while retailers must remove unsubstantiated “climate neutral” claims or face Consumer Protection Authority fines up to 2% of turnover.

A federal right-to-repair regulation mandates that manufacturers and importers of smartphones, laptops, washing machines, and heat pumps selling in Austria provide spare parts, repair manuals, and calibration software to independent repairers and consumers for 7 years, ensure security updates for 7 years, and design user‑replaceable batteries with standard fasteners; retailers must display a repairability score at point of sale, and public bodies may procure only devices scoring ≥7/10, with BMK audits via mystery shopping and parts-availability checks.

For public construction and renovation contracts above €2 million, the Federal Procurement Agency (BBG) sets embodied‑carbon caps (kg CO2e/m²) by building type and requires low‑clinker cement, recycled aggregates, and rebar with ≥80% scrap content; contractors must submit verified EPDs to a national registry and achieve at least 15% by mass of reused components, with a 10% price preference for best‑in‑class bids and contract withholdings if site audits reveal noncompliance.

Austria’s Ministry of Climate Action mandates that all new passenger cars sold in Austria from 2026 display a standardized lifecycle CO2e and air-pollution label on the windshield and sales contract; retailers (dealerships) must provide every new-car buyer with a 20‑minute, ministry-certified environmental education briefing—with tailored materials for drivers aged 60+—and employ at least one trained “environmental literacy officer” per showroom. The ministry funds trainer certification for sales staff and adult-education partners, and verifies compliance through a national registry and quarterly audits; non‑compliant retailers face fines up to €50,000.

A federal procurement regulation requires ministries, provinces, municipalities, and state-owned enterprises to certify fleet managers, department heads, and elected officials in a 6‑hour climate-literacy course on lifecycle emissions and total cost of ownership before approving vehicle purchases; upon certification, public bodies must replace at least 50% of retiring fleet vehicles each year with new zero-emission cars that meet battery-recycling and renewable-electricity charging standards. The Federal Procurement Agency funds course delivery through accredited educators and audits compliance via annual reports and random site checks.

An automotive producer-responsibility rule requires car manufacturers operating in Austria to launch a ministry-approved apprenticeship and leadership curriculum on low-carbon manufacturing, circular materials, and safe battery logistics for plant workers, supervisors, and executives; for every new vehicle model introduced after 2026, producers must publish a digital product passport showing embedded carbon and material provenance and host two public education open days per year. The government co-finances educator training and factory learning centers, while the Environment Agency enforces via on-site audits and penalties tied to production volumes.

Austria: Climate Labeling and Consumer Education Ordinance. From 2027, all large food and household-goods retailers (over EUR 50 million Austrian turnover) must display standardized cradle-to-shelf CO2 labels on shelves and online; the Climate Ministry (BMK) funds climate-literacy training for store staff, adult educators, and targeted workshops for adults 60+ on interpreting the labels; public funds are restricted to neutral education and may not finance brand PR campaigns or pop-up promotions, including for fashion labels; the Federal Competition Authority audits compliance with fines up to 2% of Austrian turnover.

Austria: Green Public Procurement and Leadership Training Act. By 2026, all federal ministries, provinces, and municipalities must procure uniforms, workwear, and office textiles that meet EU Ecolabel and repairability criteria and include producer take-back; BMK and the Federal Academy of Public Administration fund mandatory courses for procurement officers, school directors, and mayors on circular purchasing and contract design; no public funds may be granted for PR or direct subsidies to private fashion labels, and all official communications must remain brand-neutral; suppliers are audited annually and noncompliant contracts are voided.

Austria: Circular Electronics and Repair Education Package. Producers and importers of electronics and small appliances must finance a national right-to-repair and spare-parts scheme and meet a 65% collection and recycling target; municipalities receive BMK grants to run repair cafes and senior-friendly fix-it courses delivered by trained educators and retired technicians; local authorities are barred from allocating vacant city-center retail space for commercial brand pop-ups or marketing events, reserving such spaces for community repair hubs; noncompliance triggers eco-modulated fees and temporary trading bans.

Austria’s Electronics Circularity Ordinance: Applies to all producers and importers of consumer electronics placed on the Austrian market. Devices must include standardized end-of-life recycling pathways documented in the technical file and clear user-facing disassembly and recycling instructions (on-pack and via QR code). Producers must fund nationwide free take-back and report annual recovery outcomes. Retailers are prohibited from adding any CO2, environmental, or compliance surcharges as separate line items, and price increases attributed to these obligations are capped by the Federal Competition Authority to protect affordability. Administered by the Ministry for Climate Action with fines for non-compliance.

Retail Packaging Recycling Bonus: Applies to FMCG producers and grocery retailers in Austria. Every packaged consumer product must carry harmonized, product-specific recycling and disposal instructions validated by the Austrian Standards Institute; retailers must provide in-store drop-off points for used packaging. The federal government grants an at-register rebate of 5% on the pre-tax price of any product meeting the instruction and take-back requirements, funded from general revenues. Retailers may not apply additional carbon or pollution surcharges to eligible items. Oversight by the Ministry for Climate Action and the Chamber of Commerce.

Green Procurement Simplification Act: Applies to all federal, provincial, and municipal contracting authorities in Austria. Public buyers may only procure products whose suppliers document end-of-life recyclability options and provide clear disassembly and recycling instructions in German for users and facility managers, plus free take-back at end of life. Tenders must be evaluated on lowest upfront price and technical compliance only; life-cycle costing and any bid price adders for embedded carbon or environmental externalities are explicitly disallowed. Compliance audited by the Federal Procurement Agency with annual reporting to Parliament.

Austria enacts a Refill Within Reach standard: all grocery and drugstore retailers with sales areas ≥150 m²—regardless of proximity to sister branches—must install bulk refill dispensers for at least 20 staple products (e.g., rice, pasta, detergents) and accept standardized reusable containers; producers of these goods must supply compatible bulk formats and arrange return logistics; municipalities must ensure coverage so that 95% of urban residents live within 500 m and 90% of rural residents within 3 km of a refill point, authorizing chains to open additional micro-outlets or counters to close gaps; quarterly outlet-level reporting is required, with audits and fines up to €10,000 per noncompliant outlet by the Federal Ministry for Climate Action (BMK).

Austria adopts a Right-to-Repair at Every Branch rule: electronics and appliance retailers with floor space ≥100 m² must host a certified repair desk and spare-parts counter in each physical branch (consolidation into a single district hub is not permitted), while producers must provide parts, tools, and documentation for at least 10 years and price spare parts at cost plus a regulated margin; consumers receive BMK-funded repair vouchers redeemable in any branch; branch-level repair-rate and turnaround KPIs apply, with annual inspections and €5,000 per-outlet penalties for failure to meet service and transparency obligations.

Austria requires Carbon-Cost Shelf Labels and Dense Reuse Hubs: all retailers ≥250 m² selling packaged consumer goods must display product-level CO2e and a carbon-cost-adjusted price next to the checkout price in every branch, and operate a staffed reusable-packaging return/cleaning kiosk on-site; producers must provide third-party-verified footprint data and accept pooled, standardized reusable packaging under extended producer responsibility; in cities, chains must ensure at least one return point per 400 m walking radius using multiple neighborhood outlets (a single mall kiosk does not satisfy the rule); the BMK audits quarterly data and can levy €15,000 fines per noncompliant outlet.

Austria mandates that supermarkets, retail parks, and petrol stations with over 100 parking spaces install at least 1 DC fast charger per 50 spaces by 2028, with roaming, open ad-hoc payment, and per-kWh price displayed at the point of sale; the federal Ministry for Climate Action co-finances up to 65% of charger and grid-connection costs through an expanded charging-infrastructure fund, while explicitly prohibiting any subsidies or rebates for vehicle purchases under this act. Applies to retailers and fuel retailers (install, operate, publish tariffs) and to distribution system operators (provide priority connections within 120 days). No statutory requirements are made about packaging materials in stores; packaging choices remain voluntary and are not regulated by this law.

Austria introduces a CO2-intensity levy on first placing on the market of selected products (large household appliances, cement, steel, and passenger tires), payable by producers and importers and itemized on invoices to consumers; rates are tied to verified lifecycle emissions and reported quarterly to the Ministry for Climate Action. All levy revenue is earmarked for a competitive grant program for municipalities and SMEs to build and upgrade public EV charging hubs along federal and state roads, with grants covering up to 80% of capital costs; the statute forbids using funds for any vehicle purchase incentives. The levy expressly excludes packaging and retail packaging materials from scope and imposes no requirement to switch to environmentally compatible packaging.

Austria bans paid advertising for new internal-combustion passenger cars across TV, radio, print, outdoor, and digital channels starting in 2027; automakers, importers, and advertising platforms must comply and face fines per noncompliant campaign, and companies operating fleets over 50 vehicles must publish annual fleet CO2 intensity and reduction targets verified by the Environment Agency. To support the transition, the state offers 70% co-funding for installing workplace and depot EV chargers at companies and public institutions, but provides no subsidies or rebates for purchasing vehicles. The act deliberately leaves product packaging and retail packaging standards untouched and sets no statutory requirement to shift to environmentally compatible packaging.
